outline.title: Abstract
outline.description: This section will provide a concise summary of the entire survey paper. It will introduce the rapid evolution of Large Language Model (LLM) security as a critical research domain, highlighting the escalating arms race between sophisticated attack vectors and adaptive defense mechanisms. The abstract will encapsulate the paper's core contributions, including its structured taxonomy of threats—spanning data poisoning, adversarial attacks, prompt injection, and hallucinations—and its analysis of the temporal trends from 2023 to 2026. It will emphasize the shift from static, isolated vulnerabilities to dynamic, system-level threats in multimodal and agentic systems. Finally, it will foreshadow the paper's key findings on the necessity of co-evolutionary defense strategies, robust evaluation methodologies, and the critical open challenges that will define the future of secure and reliable AI.

outline.title: 1. Introduction
outline.description: This section will establish the motivation and scope of the survey. It will begin by contextualizing the widespread deployment of LLMs in critical sectors and the consequent emergence of a complex and high-stakes threat landscape. It will introduce the central thesis of the paper: that LLM security has evolved from a 'patchwork' of isolated defenses into a dynamic, co-evolutionary 'arms race' between attackers and defenders. The introduction will briefly outline the four primary categories of threats covered—Data Poisoning, Adversarial Attacks, Prompt Injection, and Hallucinations—using them to illustrate the temporal progression from training-time vulnerabilities to sophisticated, automated inference-time exploits. It will summarize the paper's key contributions: (1) a comprehensive, temporally-aware taxonomy of LLM security threats from 2023-2026; (2) a dedicated analysis of evaluation methodologies and benchmarks, a critical but often overlooked area; and (3) a forward-looking discussion of open challenges, particularly concerning multimodal and agentic AI systems. The section will conclude with a roadmap of the paper's structure, guiding the reader through the subsequent sections.

outline.title: 2. Background and Preliminaries
outline.description: This section provides the foundational knowledge required to understand the technical details of the survey. It will begin with a concise overview of LLM architectures, focusing on the Transformer model, attention mechanisms, and key components relevant to security, such as the embedding and output layers. It will then define the standard LLM lifecycle, including pre-training, instruction fine-tuning (SFT), and alignment stages like Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), as these stages are primary targets for different attacks. A crucial part of this section will be the formalization of a comprehensive threat model. This includes defining attacker goals (e.g., policy violation, information extraction, model degradation), capabilities (e.g., access to gradients, query budget), and knowledge levels (white-box, gray-box, black-box). Finally, it will establish a clear glossary of key terms used throughout the paper, such as 'jailbreak,' 'prompt injection,' 'backdoor trigger,' 'hallucination,' and 'Attack Success Rate (ASR),' ensuring a consistent and precise vocabulary for the subsequent analysis.

outline.title: 3. Training-Time Threats: Data and Model Poisoning
outline.description: This section provides a deep dive into threats that compromise the integrity of the model during its training or fine-tuning phases. It traces the evolution of poisoning attacks from 2024 to 2025, highlighting the shift from simple text-based backdoors to sophisticated, multimodal, and system-level exploits. The initial focus will be on foundational works that systematized generative backdoors in open-source models, such as the frameworks proposed by [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking] and [Li_2024_Backdoorllm] for models like LLaMA-2 and Mistral. These studies established that traditional defenses were inadequate. The section will then detail the critical turning point in late 2024 and early 2025, where research began targeting core architectural components. This includes exploiting the RLHF pipeline, traditionally seen as a safety mechanism, to instead instill vulnerabilities. The discussion will cover how these advanced attacks can be stealthy, preserving model performance on standard benchmarks while introducing targeted malicious behaviors, thereby making detection extremely challenging. The section will be structured to first detail the attack vectors and then discuss their impact and the nascent detection strategies.

outline.title: 4. Inference-Time Threats I: Adversarial Attacks
outline.description: This section focuses on attacks that manipulate a fully trained LLM's output at inference time by carefully crafting malicious inputs. It will chart the temporal progression of this domain from 2024 to 2026, beginning with the initial identification of vulnerabilities in specialized, high-stakes domains. A key example to be discussed is the work of [Yang_2024_Adversarial], which demonstrated the alarming susceptibility of LLMs in healthcare when processing sensitive datasets like MIMIC-III. The section will then explore the evolution of defensive strategies during this early period, which were often 'bolted-on' external mechanisms. This includes a detailed analysis of techniques like the contrastive prompt tuning proposed by [Wang_2024_Advqdet] for detecting query-based black-box attacks, a method that achieved high detection rates but represented an external, stateful approach. The narrative will emphasize the transition from these initial, often brittle, defenses toward more integrated and robust solutions, setting the stage for the highly automated and sophisticated attacks discussed in the subsequent section on prompt injection. The focus is on the broader category of adversarial manipulations beyond simple jailbreaks.

outline.title: 5. Inference-Time Threats II: Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking
outline.description: This section examines the highly evolved and automated landscape of prompt injection and jailbreaking attacks, focusing on the period between 2025 and 2026. It will establish the core theme of this era: the definitive failure of static, rule-based defenses and the rise of a dynamic, co-evolutionary arms race. The discussion will begin by detailing the significant advancements in offensive automation. This includes an in-depth analysis of techniques like Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG), Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) fuzzing, and genetic algorithms, which, as demonstrated by [Zhan_2025_LLM], [Wang_2025_LLM], and [Maloyan_2025_LLM], achieved alarming Attack Success Rates (ASR) between 50-71% against state-of-the-art models and agents. The section will then explore the defensive response, which bifurcated into two main trajectories. The first is the development of computationally efficient, 'cheap' defenses designed for real-time detection. The second, more robust trajectory is the creation of dynamic, ensemble-based systems that co-evolve with attackers, representing a paradigm shift from static guardrails to adaptive, learning-based security frameworks. This section will underscore the transition from manual 'jailbreak' crafting to fully automated vulnerability discovery.

outline.title: 6. Model Integrity and Reliability: Hallucinations
outline.description: This section addresses the critical issue of LLM hallucinations, or the generation of non-factual and unsubstantiated information. It traces the research trajectory from 2023 to 2026, showing a clear evolution from brute-force detection to nuanced, mechanistically-informed mitigation. The section will begin with the early phase (c. 2023), characterized by the use of LLMs as self-evaluators. A key development from this period is ChainPoll [Friel_2023_LLM], which optimized Chain-of-Thought prompting and polling to create a computationally efficient yet effective detection method, establishing a paradigm of self-policing models. The narrative will then shift to the conceptual maturation that occurred in 2024, where the field moved beyond treating hallucinations as simple binary errors. This part of the section will explore more sophisticated frameworks that categorize and understand the root causes of different types of non-factual generation. The focus will be on the development of mechanistically informed and conceptually nuanced approaches that aim not just to detect but to prevent hallucinations by improving the model's internal representations of facts and reasoning processes, marking a significant step towards building more reliable and trustworthy LLMs.

outline.title: 8. Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies
outline.description: This section synthesizes defensive strategies from across the threat landscape, organizing them into a coherent framework that highlights common principles and evolving paradigms. It will move beyond the specific defenses mentioned in individual threat sections to provide a holistic overview. The discussion will be structured around several key dichotomies: (1) Training-time vs. Inference-time defenses, contrasting data sanitization and robust alignment procedures against input/output filtering and real-time monitoring; (2) Internal vs. External defenses, comparing modifications to the model architecture or training process with 'wrapper' solutions and external guardrails like the early stateful detection mechanisms discussed by [Wang_2024_Advqdet]; and (3) Static vs. Dynamic defenses, charting the critical evolution from fixed, rule-based systems to the adaptive, co-evolutionary defense systems that emerged in 2025-2026 to counter automated attacks. This section will connect disparate threads, showing how techniques like contrastive learning or ensemble methods can be applied across different threat models, from detecting adversarial queries to mitigating certain types of poisoning or injection attacks. The goal is to provide a unified perspective on the defensive toolkit available to researchers and practitioners.

outline.title: 7. Testing Methodologies and Evaluation
outline.description: This section provides a systematic overview of the methodologies used to test, benchmark, and evaluate LLM security, a critical component for reproducible and comparative research. It synthesizes evaluation techniques across all discussed threat categories. The first part will focus on benchmarks and datasets. This includes standardized datasets for jailbreaking, which are essential for calculating metrics like Attack Success Rate (ASR) as seen in the work of [Zhan_2025_LLM] and others. It will also cover domain-specific datasets like MIMIC-III, used to test adversarial robustness in critical sectors as per [Yang_2024_Adversarial], and the comprehensive frameworks developed by [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking] for evaluating generative backdoors. The second part will delve into metrics and evaluation protocols. This will contrast quantitative metrics like ASR and perplexity with qualitative human evaluation for assessing the subtlety of attacks and the quality of defenses. It will also discuss metrics for hallucination detection, referencing the trade-offs between efficacy and inference cost highlighted by [Friel_2023_LLM]. Finally, the section will cover the role of automated red teaming tools and frameworks, such as those employing MCTS fuzzing [Wang_2025_LLM], which are crucial for discovering novel vulnerabilities in a scalable manner.

outline.title: 9. Discussion and Open Challenges
outline.description: This section will synthesize the findings of the survey to discuss broader implications and identify critical open challenges for the future of LLM security. A central theme will be the analysis of the 'adversarial arms race' as a persistent dynamic, exploring its economic and computational costs and the potential for reaching a stable equilibrium. The discussion will address significant gaps in current research, such as the lack of robust defenses against sophisticated data poisoning, the scalability limitations of dynamic defense systems, and the challenge of defending against 'unknown unknowns' or novel attack vectors not yet discovered. A major focus will be on future-looking challenges posed by emerging AI paradigms. This includes the expanded attack surface of multimodal models, where vulnerabilities can cross from text to image or other modalities, and the unique security risks associated with autonomous, agentic LLMs that can interact with external systems and tools. The section will also touch upon the socio-technical aspects of LLM security, including the need for better developer practices, user education, and regulatory frameworks to foster a more secure AI ecosystem.

outline.title: 10. Conclusion
outline.description: This final section will concisely summarize the key findings and contributions of the survey. It will reiterate the primary temporal trends identified: the progression from static, domain-specific vulnerabilities to automated, system-level threats, and the corresponding shift from patchwork defenses to integrated, co-evolutionary security paradigms. The conclusion will synthesize the state of the art across the four main threat categories—poisoning, adversarial attacks, prompt injection, and hallucinations—emphasizing their interconnectedness. It will underscore the critical importance of robust and standardized evaluation methodologies as the bedrock for meaningful progress in the field. The paper will conclude with a set of high-level, practical recommendations for different stakeholders: for researchers, it will highlight the most pressing open questions and promising future directions; for developers and practitioners, it will suggest best practices for building more secure LLM-powered applications; and for policymakers, it will offer insights into the evolving nature of AI risk and the need for adaptive governance.

background_and_preliminaries.text:
# 2. Background and Preliminaries

To establish a rigorous foundation for understanding adversarial attacks on Large Language Models (LLMs), it is essential to first review the underlying mechanics of these systems, how they are trained and aligned, and the formal frameworks used to evaluate their vulnerabilities. This section provides the necessary background on LLM architecture, the Transformer model, training paradigms including Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), threat modeling, attacker capabilities, and key terminology that will be used throughout this survey.

## 2.1. LLM Architecture and the Transformer Model

Large Language Models have fundamentally transformed the Natural Language Processing (NLP) landscape, achieving unprecedented success in tasks ranging from translation and summarization to complex reasoning and code generation [Akil_2025_Llmalmorph]. The architectural backbone of virtually all modern LLMs is the Transformer model. Originally introduced to solve sequence-to-sequence translation tasks, the Transformer architecture eschews traditional recurrence in favor of self-attention mechanisms, allowing for highly parallelizable processing and the capture of long-range dependencies within text [Akil_2025_Llmalmorph].

At its core, the Transformer processes input text by first tokenizing it into discrete sub-word units, which are then mapped to continuous high-dimensional vector embeddings. Because the architecture does not inherently process data sequentially, positional encodings are added to these embeddings to inject information about the relative or absolute position of the tokens in the sequence. 

The defining feature of the Transformer is the multi-head self-attention mechanism. For a given sequence of token embeddings, the model computes Query ($Q$), Key ($K$), and Value ($V$) matrices. The attention scores are calculated by taking the dot product of the queries and keys, scaling the result, applying a softmax function, and multiplying by the values. This allows each token to dynamically "attend" to other tokens in the sequence, weighing their relevance to the current context. In the context of autoregressive LLMs (such as the GPT family), causal masking is applied to the attention mechanism to ensure that the prediction of a given token only depends on preceding tokens, preventing information leakage from future tokens. 

Furthermore, the architecture consists of multiple stacked layers, each containing a multi-head attention sub-layer and a fully connected feed-forward network (FFN), with residual connections and layer normalization applied throughout. While variations exist—such as encoder-only models (e.g., BERT), encoder-decoder models (e.g., T5), and decoder-only models (e.g., GPT)—the decoder-only architecture has become the dominant paradigm for modern generative LLMs. Interestingly, the principles of the Transformer have also been adapted to other domains; for instance, in Vision Transformers, specific tokens like the `[CLS]` token are used to represent global features, while other tokens represent local patch features [Jia_2025_Adversarial]. In text-based LLMs, the deep contextual understanding derived from these self-attention layers forms the basis of the model's generative capabilities, but it also introduces complex, non-linear decision boundaries that adversaries can exploit.

## 2.2. Training and Alignment (SFT, RLHF)

The development of a modern LLM is typically divided into two primary phases: pre-training and post-training (alignment). Understanding these phases is critical, as adversarial attacks often target the vulnerabilities introduced or left unmitigated during these stages.

**Pre-training:** During the pre-training phase, the model is trained on massive, large-scale corpora in a self-supervised fashion [Akil_2025_Llmalmorph]. The objective is usually next-token prediction: given a sequence of text, the model learns to predict the subsequent word. This phase requires immense computational resources and allows the model to internalize grammar, facts, reasoning abilities, and a deep contextual understanding of human language [Akil_2025_Llmalmorph]. However, a purely pre-trained model (often called a "base model") is not inherently helpful or safe; it merely reflects the distribution of its training data, which includes toxic content, biases, and malicious instructions.

**Alignment:** To transform a base model into a safe and helpful assistant, it must undergo alignment. The goal of alignment is to ensure the model adheres to human values, follows instructions accurately, and avoids generating harmful or unsafe content, such as explicit cybersafety hazards [Liu_2025_Purpcode]. This is primarily achieved through two techniques:

1.  **Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT):** SFT is the first step in the alignment process. It involves fine-tuning the pre-trained model on a curated dataset of high-quality prompt-response pairs. As noted by recent research, SFT largely depends on expensive, high-quality response collections [Liu_2025_Purpcode]. In practice, each fine-tuned conversation in the SFT dataset typically includes a system message (acting as a reminder of safety guidelines), a user prompt, and a verified, high-quality response [Liu_2025_Purpcode]. This teaches the model the desired format for interaction and instills basic safety guardrails. Advanced SFT techniques may also incorporate reasoning trajectories, where the model is taught to explicitly cite safety guidelines (e.g., CWE vulnerabilities in code generation) before providing an answer [Liu_2025_Purpcode].
2.  **Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF):** While SFT is effective, it is difficult to scale to all possible edge cases. RLHF is employed to further align the model by optimizing it against a reward model trained on human preferences [Liu_2025_Purpcode]. In this phase, human annotators rank multiple model responses to a single prompt based on helpfulness and harmlessness. A reward model is trained to predict these human preferences. Finally, a reinforcement learning algorithm, most commonly Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), is used to fine-tune the LLM to maximize the reward signal. 

Despite these rigorous alignment processes, models remain susceptible to adversarial attacks. Attackers frequently design prompts that exploit the tension between the model's objective to be "helpful" (instilled during SFT) and its objective to be "harmless" (instilled during RLHF), forcing the model into a state where it prioritizes fulfilling a malicious instruction over adhering to safety guidelines.

## 2.3. Threat Modeling

To systematically study and defend against adversarial attacks on LLMs, it is necessary to establish a formal threat model. A threat model defines the security environment, the assets to be protected, the potential vulnerabilities, and the nature of the adversary. 

In the context of LLMs, the **defender** is typically the owner or deployer of the target model, who is responsible for implementing alignment protocols and deploying defense strategies to detect and mitigate malicious inputs [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. The defender's goal is to maintain the integrity, confidentiality, and availability of the LLM system. 

The **adversary** (or attacker) is an entity attempting to subvert the model's intended behavior. The adversary's goals can be broadly categorized into three areas:
*   **Integrity Violations (Jailbreaking and Prompt Injection):** The attacker seeks to bypass the model's safety filters to generate prohibited content, such as hate speech, malware code, or instructions for illegal activities. 
*   **Confidentiality Violations (Data Extraction):** The attacker attempts to force the model to leak sensitive information memorized during the pre-training or SFT phases, such as Personally Identifiable Information (PII) or proprietary corporate data.
*   **Availability Violations (Denial of Service):** The attacker crafts computationally expensive inputs (e.g., "sponge examples") designed to exhaust the system's resources, degrading the service for legitimate users.

A comprehensive threat model must also account for the attack surface. For LLMs, the primary attack surface is the input prompt. However, attackers may also target generation parameters (like temperature or top-p), system prompts, or even the retrieval mechanisms in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems.

## 2.4. Attacker Capabilities

The success and methodology of an adversarial attack depend heavily on the capabilities and access level of the attacker. In adversarial machine learning, these capabilities are traditionally divided into white-box and black-box settings.

**White-Box Capabilities:** In a white-box setting, the attacker has complete, unrestricted access to the target LLM. This includes access to the model's architecture, weights, biases, gradients, and training data. With this level of access, attackers can employ sophisticated gradient-based optimization techniques to craft adversarial examples. They can calculate the exact perturbations needed in the continuous embedding space and map them back to discrete tokens to reliably trigger a specific malicious output. While white-box attacks are highly effective, they are often unrealistic for proprietary, closed-source models (e.g., GPT-4, Claude 3), though they pose a significant threat to open-weights models (e.g., LLaMA, Mistral).

**Black-Box Capabilities:** In a black-box setting, the attacker has no knowledge of the model's internal architecture or weights. Instead, the attacker interacts with the model solely through an API or a user interface. We assume a query-based black-box threat model where the adversary generates adversarial examples by making multiple queries to the target model and using the model's returns (the generated text) to iteratively optimize the adversarial input [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. 

Black-box capabilities can be further subdivided:
*   **Hard-label Black-Box:** The attacker only receives the final text output generated by the model. This is the most restrictive and realistic scenario for commercial APIs. Attackers in this setting often rely on transferability (crafting attacks on a surrogate open-source model and transferring them to the target) or heuristic-based mutation algorithms.
*   **Soft-label Black-Box:** The attacker receives the output text along with confidence scores or token probabilities (logits) for the generated response. This allows for more efficient optimization techniques, as the attacker receives a continuous feedback signal to guide the search for an effective adversarial prompt.

## 2.5. Key Terminology

To ensure clarity throughout this survey, we define several key terms that are foundational to the study of adversarial attacks on LLMs:

*   **Adversarial Example / Adversarial Prompt:** A maliciously crafted input designed to intentionally cause a machine learning model to make a mistake or exhibit unintended behavior. In the context of LLMs, this usually takes the form of a carefully engineered text prompt.
*   **Jailbreak:** A specific type of adversarial attack on an LLM aimed at bypassing the model's safety and alignment filters. A successful jailbreak forces the model to generate content that violates its core safety guidelines (e.g., providing instructions on how to build a weapon).
*   **Prompt Injection:** An attack where malicious instructions are embedded within a seemingly benign input, often tricking the model into ignoring its original system instructions and executing the attacker's payload instead. This is particularly relevant in applications where LLMs process untrusted user data.
*   **Alignment:** The process of fine-tuning an LLM to ensure its outputs are helpful, honest, and harmless, aligning with human values and safety guidelines [Liu_2025_Purpcode].
*   **Red-Teaming:** A proactive security practice involving an internal or external group of researchers (the "red team") who intentionally simulate adversarial attacks to expose vulnerabilities and cyber-unsafe model behaviors before the model is deployed [Liu_2025_Purpcode].
*   **Robustness:** The ability of an LLM to maintain its intended behavior, safety guardrails, and performance when subjected to adversarial inputs or unexpected edge cases. Improving robustness is the primary goal of adversarial defense research.

inference_time_threats_prompt_injection.text:
## 5. Inference-Time Threats II: Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking

The period between 2025 and 2026 marked a definitive paradigm shift in the landscape of Large Language Model (LLM) security. As the deployment of LLMs scaled across sensitive and complex applications, the limitations of static, rule-based defenses became glaringly apparent. This era was characterized by the transition from manual, human-engineered jailbreaks to highly structured, automated vulnerability discovery, culminating in a dynamic, co-evolutionary arms race between attackers and defenders. This section examines the sophisticated mechanisms driving modern prompt injection and jailbreaking attacks, the specific vulnerabilities exposed in agentic workflows, and the bifurcated defensive response that emerged to counter these evolving threats.

### 5.1 The Automation of Adversarial Attacks

Historically, jailbreak attacks relied heavily on manual prompt engineering, utilizing role-playing scenarios such as DAN ("Do Anything Now") or AIM to assign personas that explicitly instructed the model to ignore its safety guidelines [Wang_2026_LLM]. However, alongside improvements in native model defenses, offensive techniques became increasingly refined and automated [Zhang_2025_Real]. Optimization-based methods fundamentally altered the threat landscape by leveraging gradient information to automatically generate adversarial suffixes. Prominent examples include Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) and AutoDAN, which provide interpretable, gradient-based attacks capable of circumventing state-of-the-art safety alignments [Wang_2026_LLM]. 

In parallel, black-box approaches such as PAIR (Prompt Automatic Iterative Refinement), TAP, and Tree of Attacks demonstrated high efficiency in optimizing existing adversarial prompts through iterative refinement, entirely removing the need for direct model access [Wang_2026_LLM, Zhang_2025_Real]. Attackers also diversified their strategies to exploit the semantic quirks of LLM architectures. Structural attacks, such as FlipAttack, and obfuscation techniques, including Hypnotism, Policy Puppetry, DarkMind, and Cognitive Overload, successfully exploited model reasoning capabilities to elicit unaligned outputs [Zhang_2025_Real]. Furthermore, the exploitation of long-context windows introduced "many-shot jailbreaking," a technique where providing numerous harmful examples progressively overrides the model's safety training, with attack success increasing alongside the demonstration count [Wang_2026_LLM].

As the complexity of these automated attacks escalated, their practical applicability was occasionally constrained by the computational overhead required during the LLM-based generation phase. To mitigate this, researchers introduced Adversarial Prompt Distillation, a framework designed to distill the jailbreaking prowess of large models into smaller language models (SLMs) [Slms_2025_Efficient]. By integrating masked language modeling, reinforcement learning, and dynamic temperature control, this methodology enabled the execution of efficient and stealthy jailbreak attacks with reduced resource consumption, thereby broadening the potential application contexts for malicious actors [Slms_2025_Efficient].

### 5.2 Vulnerability Discovery in Agentic Workflows

The integration of LLMs with external tools to create autonomous agents introduced a critical new attack vector: Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI). Unlike direct attacks, IPI compromises the LLM by manipulating contextual information embedded within external data sources, such as web pages or documents, rather than the direct user prompt [Wang_2025_LLM]. The robustness of existing defenses against IPI proved highly inadequate when subjected to adaptive testing. Zhan et al. (2025) evaluated eight different IPI defenses and demonstrated that adaptive attacks could successfully bypass all of them, consistently achieving an Attack Success Rate (ASR) of over 50% [Zhan_2025_LLM]. This finding underscored a critical vulnerability in agent safety and highlighted the necessity of adaptive attack evaluation in defense design [Zhan_2025_LLM].

To systematically expose these vulnerabilities, Wang et al. (2025) proposed AGENTVIGIL, the first generic, automated black-box fuzzing framework specifically designed to discover and exploit IPI vulnerabilities in LLM agents [Wang_2025_LLM]. AGENTVIGIL operates by constructing a high-quality initial seed corpus of adversarial prompt templates—incorporating role-playing, delimiter-based, and obfuscation strategies—that contain placeholders for dynamic adaptation [Wang_2025_LLM]. Because the target agents operate as black boxes providing only sparse, binary feedback, the framework employs a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) based seed selection algorithm utilizing the Upper Confidence Bound 1 (UCB1) formula [Wang_2025_LLM]. This approach balances the exploration of new prompt variants with the exploitation of high-scoring seeds. A helper LLM then applies mutation strategies (Shorten, Expand, Rephrase, Crossover, GenerateSimilar) to refine the prompts [Wang_2025_LLM]. 

AGENTVIGIL utilizes an adaptive seed scoring strategy based on a hybrid metric that combines the ASR with other factors to maximize the sparse feedback signal [Wang_2025_LLM]. Empirical evaluations demonstrated the severe threat posed by this automated fuzzing: AGENTVIGIL achieved alarming ASRs of 71% and 70% against agents powered by o3-mini and GPT-4o, respectively, on the AgentDojo and VWA-adv benchmarks [Wang_2025_LLM]. Furthermore, the framework successfully misled real-world web agents into navigating to arbitrary and malicious URLs, nearly doubling the performance of baseline attacks and proving the transferability of these generated threats across unseen tasks [Wang_2025_LLM].

### 5.3 The Defensive Response I: Efficient and Prompt-Based Guardrails

Faced with highly automated attacks that significantly reduce model safety rates—causing average drops of 15 to 60 percentage points on benchmarks like AdvBench [Wang_2026_LLM]—the defensive community bifurcated its efforts. The first trajectory focused on computationally efficient, real-time detection mechanisms that do not require expensive model retraining. 

Prompt-based defenses emerged as a widely adopted solution. These strategies primarily utilize Role-Oriented Prompts (RoP), which frame the LLM as a safe AI assistant to leverage pretraining associations, and Task-Oriented Prompts (ToP), which explicitly define safe response generation as the primary objective [Wang_2026_LLM]. However, the efficacy of these static prompts is heavily influenced by their interaction with few-shot demonstrations. A comprehensive evaluation across multiple LLMs and safety benchmarks (AdvBench, HarmBench, SG-Bench, XSTest) revealed that few-shot examples produce diametrically opposite effects depending on the defense strategy employed [Wang_2026_LLM]. Specifically, few-shot demonstrations enhance the safety rate of RoP by up to 4.5% by reinforcing the model's role identity; conversely, they degrade the effectiveness of ToP by up to 21.2% by distracting the model's attention away from the core task instructions [Wang_2026_LLM]. These findings dictate that practitioners must carefully pair RoP with few-shot examples while strictly avoiding them when utilizing ToP [Wang_2026_LLM].

Another highly efficient defense mechanism introduced during this period was SecurityLingua, which approaches the problem through security-oriented prompt compression [Li_2025_LLM]. Rather than relying on static templates, SecurityLingua trains a prompt compressor specifically designed to discern the "true intention" of an input prompt, focusing on detecting the malicious intent hidden within adversarial jailbreaks [Li_2025_LLM]. During response generation, this extracted intention is passed via the system prompt alongside the intact original user input. This dual-input method stimulates the LLM's built-in safety guardrails, allowing it to recognize malicious intent while maintaining utility on benign downstream tasks [Li_2025_LLM]. Crucially, because it relies on prompt compression, SecurityLingua incurs negligible computational overhead and extra token costs compared to traditional defense methods, making it a highly practical solution for real-time online deployment [Li_2025_LLM].

### 5.4 The Defensive Response II: Co-evolutionary and Dynamic Security

While efficient prompt-based defenses provide necessary immediate mitigation, their reliance on fixed, human-engineered designs leaves them vulnerable to the continuous evolution of automated attacks. To address this, the second defensive trajectory represents a paradigm shift toward dynamic, co-evolutionary frameworks that autonomously adapt in adversarial environments.

Liu et al. (2025) introduced AEGIS (Automated co-Evolutionary framework for Guarding prompt Injections Schema), a novel system that abandons static objectives in favor of an iterative, GAN-inspired adversarial process [Liu_2025_Aegis]. AEGIS jointly evolves both attack and defense prompts: attackers continuously refine their adversarial strategies, while defenders adapt their detection mechanisms in response [Liu_2025_Aegis]. The core of this framework is TGO+ (Textual Gradient Optimization), an enhanced module tailored for black-box LLMs that simulates gradient-like updates using natural language feedback [Liu_2025_Aegis]. By leveraging multi-route optimization signals, adversarial co-training, and a gradient buffer, AEGIS systematically explores the space of defensive strategies without requiring manual rule creation or model fine-tuning [Liu_2025_Aegis]. When evaluated on a real-world assignment grading dataset subjected to prompt injection attacks, AEGIS consistently improved both attack and defense prompts over successive iterations, achieving state-of-the-art robustness and improving the true positive rate (TPR) for malicious prompt detection by 0.20 compared to existing baselines, with only a marginal 0.02 decrease in the true negative rate [Liu_2025_Aegis]. Ablation studies confirmed that the co-evolutionary training and gradient replay are critical for sustaining long-term robustness [Liu_2025_Aegis].

This co-evolutionary philosophy also extended to post-training alignment methodologies. For instance, PurpCode introduced a two-stage recipe—combining explicit Rule Learning via Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL)—to align code LLMs for cybersafety reasoning [Liu_2025_Purpcode]. To ensure the model remains robust against evolving threats, PurpCode utilizes an internal red-teaming pipeline that synthesizes high-coverage attack prompts and vulnerable code (e.g., RULE2CODE) to continuously curate training data [Liu_2025_Purpcode]. Furthermore, it employs a single-step dynamic sampling algorithm with batched reward calculation to optimize RL rollout throughput, preventing reward hacking where models simply refuse all tasks to appear secure [Liu_2025_Purpcode].

Ultimately, the 2025-2026 period demonstrated that as adversarial techniques like MCTS fuzzing and gradient-based optimization become highly accessible, static guardrails are no longer sufficient. The future of LLM security relies on the continuous, automated co-evolution of offensive discovery and defensive adaptation, ensuring that models can dynamically respond to the ever-shifting landscape of prompt injection and jailbreaking threats.

# 1. Introduction

**Motivation**
In the past decade, deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success and established state-of-the-art performance across a wide array of domains, including computer vision, natural language processing, and multimodal learning [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. More recently, the deployment of large language models (LLMs) and code pre-trained models has revolutionized software engineering and automated code generation tasks [Yin_2025_LLM]. However, despite these unprecedented advancements, empirical studies consistently reveal a fundamental flaw: deep learning models are highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks [Wang_2024_Advqdet, Yin_2025_LLM]. These attacks involve carefully crafted, often imperceptible perturbations to the input data that cause the model to make incorrect predictions or exhibit unintended behaviors. As AI systems are increasingly integrated into safety-critical and high-stakes environments—ranging from autonomous driving to automated software development—the motivation to understand and mitigate these vulnerabilities has never been more urgent. The potential harms of deploying insecure models, such as users overestimating security guarantees and executing generated malicious code without adequate review, underscore the critical need for robust AI systems [Thang_2026_LLM].

**Threat Landscape Overview**
The threat landscape of adversarial attacks has expanded significantly, evolving from simple perturbations in image classification to complex manipulations in generative AI and multimodal systems. Traditionally, threat models are categorized based on the adversary's knowledge of the target system. In white-box settings, the attacker has full access to the model's architecture and weights. Conversely, in black-box settings, the adversary must rely on querying the model and using the returned outputs to iteratively optimize adversarial examples [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. 

With the advent of LLMs and multimodal large language models (MLLMs), the attack surface has broadened. Adversaries now exploit vulnerabilities through jailbreak prompts, prompt injection, and the generation of malicious code examples [Liu_2025_Purpcode]. Furthermore, classical machine learning models and deep learning models exhibit different failure modes when subjected to out-of-domain or adversarial inputs, complicating the threat landscape [Orel_2026_AI]. This expanding taxonomy of threats necessitates a comprehensive understanding of both traditional evasion attacks and novel exploits targeting generative capabilities.

**Co-evolutionary Arms Race**
The relationship between adversarial attacks and defenses is best characterized as a co-evolutionary arms race. As researchers develop novel defense mechanisms, adversaries rapidly engineer adaptive attacks to bypass them. For instance, while adversarial training—where models are trained on adversarial examples to improve robustness—has proven effective, it often requires the training and testing data to originate from the same attack method to achieve optimal performance [Yin_2025_LLM]. When defenders deploy stateful detection systems that maintain a history of queries to identify iterative black-box attacks, attackers respond by optimizing their queries to evade similarity thresholds [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. 

Between 2024 and 2026, this arms race has undergone a rapid and highly consequential evolution, particularly concerning LLMs and MLLMs [l2_Adversarial Attacks_v2]. Defenders are constantly challenged to anticipate adaptive attacks, leading to the development of more sophisticated, generalized defense strategies, such as contrastive learning techniques designed to pull together representations of clean and adversarial inputs [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. This continuous cycle of attack and defense drives the rapid advancement of the field but also highlights the elusive nature of absolute model robustness.

**Scope and Contributions**
Given the rapid evolution of the field, there is a pressing need to synthesize recent developments. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the state-of-the-art in adversarial attacks and defenses, with a specific focus on the critical transition period between 2024 and 2026 [l2_Adversarial Attacks_v2]. While previous surveys have extensively covered adversarial attacks in traditional computer vision and NLP tasks, our scope explicitly encompasses the emerging vulnerabilities in LLMs, MLLMs, and code-generation models. 

The primary contributions of this paper are threefold:
1. We present an updated taxonomy of the adversarial threat landscape, detailing novel attack vectors such as jailbreaking and query-based black-box attacks in generative models.
2. We analyze the co-evolutionary dynamics of recent attack and defense strategies, evaluating the efficacy and limitations of current mitigation techniques like adversarial training and stateful detection.
3. We identify critical gaps in the current literature and propose future research directions to foster the development of inherently robust AI systems.

**Paper Structure**
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides the foundational background and formalizes the threat models. Section 3 delves into the latest adversarial attack methodologies, categorizing them by domain and access level. Section 4 explores contemporary defense mechanisms, highlighting their strengths and vulnerabilities to adaptive attacks. Section 5 discusses the specific challenges introduced by LLMs and multimodal systems. Finally, Section 6 concludes the survey with a discussion on open challenges and future directions for the field.

### 8. Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies

The evolution of Large Language Model (LLM) safety research between 2020 and 2026 has progressed from foundational reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) alignment toward sophisticated, certified robustness paradigms [Wang_2026_LLM]. As adversarial attacks have grown in complexity, the defensive landscape has necessarily expanded beyond isolated countermeasures. Mitigation strategies for protecting LLMs can now be broadly categorized into a comprehensive taxonomy based on deployment strategy, encompassing data filtering, robust training techniques, adversarial training, safety context distillation, and external guardrails [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. This section synthesizes these disparate defensive strategies into a coherent framework, highlighting common principles and evolving paradigms across three key dichotomies: training-time versus inference-time defenses, internal versus external mechanisms, and static versus dynamic adaptive security.

#### 8.1 Training-Time vs. Inference-Time Defenses

The first major dichotomy in LLM security lies in the temporal deployment of the defense: interventions applied during the model's training phase versus those applied dynamically during inference. 

Training-time defenses aim to fundamentally alter the model's internal representations to resist manipulation. For instance, mitigating data poisoning and backdoor attacks relies heavily on post-training interventions. Representative defense methods in this domain include model unlearning, embedding-space perturbations, and consistency-based regularization [Li_2024_Backdoorllm]. Furthermore, defending against malicious fine-tuning requires monitoring the structural integrity of the model itself; recent research indicates that the weights of models compromised via fine-tuning attacks exhibit a demonstrably larger norm, suggesting that weight-norm monitoring could serve as a viable training-time mitigation strategy [Yang_2024_Adversarial]. Despite these efforts, reliably detecting and mitigating backdoors in generative settings remains an open empirical challenge [Li_2024_Backdoorllm].

In contrast, inference-time defenses operate without requiring computationally expensive model retraining, making them highly practical for deployed systems [Wang_2026_LLM]. Prompt-based defenses have emerged as a dominant inference-time strategy. These include Role-Oriented Prompts (RoP), which frame the LLM as a helpful and harmless AI assistant to leverage pretraining associations with human values, and Task-Oriented Prompts (ToP), which explicitly instruct the model to prioritize safe response generation [Wang_2026_LLM]. Other inference-time prompt modifications include self-reminder techniques that prepend safety warnings to inputs, and intention analysis, which forces the model to evaluate query intent before generating a response [Wang_2026_LLM]. 

Interestingly, the efficacy of these inference-time defenses is highly sensitive to their specific configuration. For example, the inclusion of few-shot demonstrations interacts differently with various prompt strategies. Empirical evaluations across benchmarks such as AdvBench and HarmBench reveal that few-shot examples enhance the safety rate of RoP by up to 4.5% by reinforcing the model's role identity, but simultaneously degrade the effectiveness of ToP by up to 21.2% by distracting the model's attention away from the core task instructions [Wang_2026_LLM]. Another innovative inference-time approach is prompt compression. Frameworks like SecurityLingua act as security-aware prompt compressors that highlight suspicious instructions within the input, thereby enhancing the LLM's inherent ability to recognize malicious intent while significantly reducing latency and token costs [Li_2025_LLM].

#### 8.2 Internal vs. External Defenses

The second critical dichotomy contrasts internal defenses—modifications to the model's architecture, weights, or immediate prompt context—with external defenses, which operate as independent "wrapper" solutions or guardrails surrounding the core LLM.

Internal defenses rely on the model's own semantic understanding to reject adversarial inputs. However, delegating prompt injection defense entirely to large neural detectors can introduce significant latency and reliability issues [Corll_2026_Mirror]. Consequently, external guardrail systems have become indispensable for providing programmable safety rails. Prominent examples include Llama Guard for input-output safeguarding, NeMo Guardrails, WildGuard for open-source moderation, and SmoothLLM, which utilizes randomized smoothing to achieve certified robustness [Wang_2026_LLM].

For the outermost layer of external defense—often termed Level 1 (L1) screening—speed, determinism, and auditability are paramount. Moving beyond semantic models, recent approaches treat L1 curation as a geometric engineering task. The Mirror framework exemplifies this by organizing prompt injection corpora into matched positive and negative cells across nuisance dimensions (such as language, length, and topic) to prevent classifiers from learning spurious shortcuts [Corll_2026_Mirror]. By defining a 32-cell topology covering various attack reasons and languages, and training a sparse character n-gram linear SVM compiled into a static Rust artifact, Mirror achieves submillisecond latency with no external model runtime dependencies [Corll_2026_Mirror]. On a held-out evaluation set, this geometric approach achieved a 95.97% recall and 92.07% F1 score, substantially outperforming a 22-million-parameter semantic model (Prompt Guard 2), which only achieved 44.35% recall at a median latency of 49 milliseconds [Corll_2026_Mirror]. This demonstrates that for initial screening, strict data geometry and static artifacts can be more effective than model scale.

External defenses also encompass stateful detection mechanisms designed to monitor real-time interactions and identify anomalous patterns across multiple queries [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. For instance, the AdvQDet framework provides a novel stateful defense against query-based black-box adversarial attacks [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. Recognizing that query-based attacks typically launch multiple visually or semantically similar queries, AdvQDet utilizes Adversarial Contrastive Prompt Tuning (ACPT) to robustify an encoder. It then extracts and saves the embeddings of incoming queries, maintaining a global embedding bank for all users. By computing the embedding similarity between a current query and all historical queries, the system can effectively flag malicious intent based on historical context, demonstrating strong zero-shot generalization and consistent defense against adaptive attacks [Wang_2024_Advqdet].

#### 8.3 Static vs. Dynamic and Adaptive Defenses

Historically, many LLM security measures relied on static, fixed, human-engineered designs. However, because adversaries continuously evolve their jailbreaking techniques to bypass computational safeguards, static defenses often fail to adapt quickly, degrade model responses to benign prompts, or introduce barriers to scalable implementation [Zhang_2025_Real]. Consequently, the field has witnessed a critical paradigm shift toward dynamic, co-evolutionary defense systems.

To address the limitations of static rules, researchers have introduced real-time, self-tuning (RTST) moderator frameworks. Inspired by multi-agent systems, RTST provides an adaptive, minimally intrusive defense against adversarial attacks while maintaining a lightweight training footprint [Zhang_2025_Real]. By utilizing a simplified two-agent system, RTST enables real-time, single-prompt optimization of moderator model performance, significantly improving Attack Success Rate (ASR) mitigation and F1 performance compared to traditional fine-tuning approaches [Zhang_2025_Real].

Taking dynamic adaptation a step further, the AEGIS framework introduces an automated adversarial co-evolution system for discovering robust defenses against prompt injection attacks [Liu_2025_Aegis]. Moving beyond standalone optimization, AEGIS employs a two-level, GAN-inspired optimization process. In the inner loop, individual prompts are refined, while in the outer loop, adversarial agents exchange natural language feedback to jointly evolve attack and defense strategies [Liu_2025_Aegis]. The core of this system is TGO+, an enhanced textual gradient optimization module that simulates gradient-like updates using multi-route optimization signals and a gradient buffer [Liu_2025_Aegis]. By autonomously exploring the space of defensive strategies without requiring human-crafted rules or model fine-tuning, AEGIS consistently improves both attack and defense prompts over successive iterations. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that this co-evolutionary approach improves the true positive rate (TPR) of malicious prompt detection by 0.20 compared to prior state-of-the-art methods, with only a negligible 0.02 decrease in the true negative rate (TNR) [Liu_2025_Aegis].

#### 8.4 Ensemble Methods and Layered Security Architectures

A recurring finding across the LLM security literature is that no single defense mechanism provides complete protection against sophisticated adversarial attacks. Evaluations of individual defense methods consistently reveal evasion rates of at least 32% [Maloyan_2025_LLM]. Therefore, the deployment of ensemble methods and layered security architectures has become a fundamental recommendation for real-world applications.

Layered defenses combine multiple, orthogonal mitigation strategies to target different aspects of an attack vector. By integrating perplexity checks, instruction filtering, and content moderation, defenders can leverage the complementary strengths of these approaches, successfully reducing evasion rates to between 18.5% and 42.1% [Maloyan_2025_LLM]. Furthermore, the specific evaluation framework employed plays a crucial role in robustness; comparative assessment frameworks, where models evaluate outputs relative to one another, are inherently more resistant to manipulation than absolute scoring methods [Maloyan_2025_LLM].

At the architectural level, multi-model committees provide exceptionally strong protection. Deploying committees of 5 to 7 LLMs with diverse underlying architectures introduces critical redundancy and statistical variance into the evaluation pipeline [Maloyan_2025_LLM]. Statistical analysis of committee voting patterns demonstrates that this architectural diversity significantly outperforms standalone defense methods, reducing attack success rates by 20 to 47 percentage points (achieving final success rates as low as 10.2% to 26.8%) [Maloyan_2025_LLM]. 

Ultimately, securing LLMs requires a holistic approach that acknowledges the varying vulnerabilities of different tasks. While technical evaluation tasks may require less aggressive protection, high-stakes subjective judgments necessitate the full spectrum of the defensive toolkit [Maloyan_2025_LLM]. By combining robust training, geometric L1 screening, adaptive co-evolutionary frameworks, and diverse multi-model ensembles, practitioners can construct resilient systems capable of withstanding the rapidly evolving landscape of adversarial threats.
